messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

For fifteen months in his mid-sixties, Phong was held captive in a shipping container. He had been working as a plumber on a large overseas construction project when local militia took him and three other men. They were kept in darkness, fed once a day, and moved between locations in the back of trucks. The worst part, Phong would later say, was the unpredictability—never knowing when the metal door would slide open, never knowing which of the armed men would be standing there. He learned to read their moods by the way they moved. A sudden step forward meant a beating. A slow turn of the head meant they might be left alone. He memorized escape routes in every container they put him in, always watching for a seam in the metal, always calculating how many seconds it would take to run.

Now, four years after his release, Phong is back at work as a plumber in a small city in Ohio. He is married, with adult children who visit on holidays. But the life he returned to has slowly become unrecognizable to him. The triggers are everywhere, and they are not always obvious. Being alone with a male customer in a basement utility room makes his throat tighten. The smell of diesel fuel from a passing truck can send him reeling. Most puzzling to him, and most distressing, is the nausea that rises without warning when he feels trapped—even in his own kitchen. He has come to believe that his body knows something his mind cannot hold.

What frightens Phong most is the way his memories behave. When he tries to tell his wife what happened—just a simple account, just the facts—the words vanish. He knows what he saw, what he heard, what he smelled, but the sentences collapse. "I can't find the words," he says, and then he stops. Other times, without any trigger he can identify, the memory plays like a film behind his eyes: the metal door sliding open, the silhouette of a man, the sound of boots on concrete. These replays leave him shaken and exhausted. After one of them, he will often feel a sharp, stabbing pain in his neck that lasts for hours.

The connection between these memories and his sense of threat has become a daily reality. After a memory replay, Phong finds himself scanning every room he enters for exits. He feels on guard even inside his own home, especially when his wife is out and he hears an unexpected noise. A sudden movement by another person—a customer reaching for a tool, his grandson jumping off the couch—makes him flinch and brace. He knows this is not normal, but the physical reaction comes before he can stop it. "My body decides before my brain does," he told his doctor.

Phong has developed a set of strategies that he knows, on some level, are keeping the problem alive. He avoids anniversaries of his capture entirely—he will not say the date aloud, and he makes sure to be working a double shift on that day. Before entering any new place, he plans an escape route. He will not sit with his back to a door. He will not let himself be alone with a male customer if there is no window in the room. These precautions feel necessary, but they have also narrowed his world. His wife has noticed that he no longer agrees to dinner at restaurants unless he has scouted the layout first. His boss has commented that he takes too long to start a job because he "walks the whole building" before touching a pipe.

The most troubling loop, from Phong's perspective, is that the more he tries to detach from the memories, the more they intrude. He has learned to push them away during the day—to focus on the wrench in his hand, the pressure in the pipe, the numbers on a bill. But when he lets his guard down, the film starts playing again. And the more the film plays, the more he feels the need to detach. He has begun to wonder if he is losing his mind. "I can't talk about it, and I can't stop seeing it," he said in his first session.

What finally brought Phong to a psychologist was an incident at work. He was in a crawlspace, alone, repairing a leak, when the homeowner—a large man—appeared at the access hatch and called down to him. Phong could not see his face, only his silhouette against the light. He froze. His heart pounded. He felt nauseous. He could not move or speak for nearly a minute. When he finally crawled out, he told the homeowner he was sick and left the job unfinished. That night, he could not sleep. The film played over and over. His neck ached. He told his wife, "I need help. I can't keep living like this." He is afraid that he will lose his job, or that his marriage will crack under the weight of his silence. But more than anything, he is afraid that the man in the hatch will keep coming back, and that one day, he will not be able to crawl out at all.
